items.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Oxygen Evolution Reaction (OER) is a fundamental process, with gold standards like RuO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> and IrO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>. Recently, it was suggested that OER could go through unconventional intermediates, −O−H, −OO−H. −O−H is formed by the direct interaction of an adsorbed O species to a metal surface atom and a proton bound to a surface oxygen. Similarly, in −OO−H, an adsorbed −OO adduct interacts with a proton on a surface oxygen. This work compares the nature of key intermediates of OER on TiO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>, RuO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>, and IrO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>(110) surfaces by Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations and Ab‐Initio Molecular Dynamics (AIMD). We rationalized the nature, the relative stability trends in vacuum and the effect of water solvation of the species. −OO−H is preferred than −OOH. −OH is preferred than −O−H except for RuO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>. We investigated the nature of the catalyst/water interfaces and the interaction of intermediates with water based on AIMD. On RuO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>, −OH and −O−H display a different interaction with water. −OO−H is quite rigid on RuO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>, while it is dynamic on IrO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> as the proton is shared between −OO and a surface oxygen atom. This study provides insights on the role of solvation to the nature of OER intermediates, that may help future studies.</jats:p>
title: Stability and Solvation of Key Intermediates of Oxygen Evolution on TiO<sub>2</sub>, RuO<sub>2</sub>, IrO<sub>2</sub> (110) Surfaces: A Comparative DFT Study

items.abstract: <jats:p>The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is a sluggish electrochemical semi-reaction, object of intense research for which a gold-standard electrocatalytic material is ruthenium dioxide (RuO2). It has been experimentally reported that an adsorbate with a superoxo character (-OO-H), where H is adsorbed on a lattice oxygen forming a hydrogen bond with the superoxo adsorbed on ruthenium, is preferred in place of the conventionally assumed peroxo (-OOH) one. Quantum chemical simulations addressed the origin of this outcome without taking into explicit consideration the application of oxidative voltage. In this work, we fill this gap by applying the grand canonical potential kinetic (GCP-K) methodology to study the potential dependent stability of OER key intermediates. Our results highlight an often-undermined aspect, as they show that the dynamic evolution in oxidative conditions of the RuO2 surface play a crucial role in determining the stability of the reaction intermediates. Furthermore, the results are also dependent on the environmental conditions, suggesting that by modifying the experimental conditions of nature and concentration of the supporting electrolyte, the order of stability can be reversed. Our results demonstrate major factors determining the relative stability of -OO-H compared to -OOH. These results could help future studies devoted to the understanding and rational design of novel electrocatalytic materials.</jats:p>
title: Unveiling the Stability of Oxygen Evolution Intermediates on RuO2 via Grand Canonical Density Functional Theory
